after.title: Preprint: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
after.authors: Sharma, C.; Oversti, S.; Stass, R.; Lucaci, A. G.; Audet, J.; Safronetz, D.; Zhao, L.; Lythgoe, K.; Katzourakis, A.; Bowden, T. A.; Lytras, S.; Ghafari, M.
after.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

after.title: Preprint: A Behaviorally Informed Patient-Facing Intervention to Promote Albuminuria Testing in Hypertension: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of KnowCKD
after.authors: Villasenor, I.; Biswas, R.; Okpara, K.; Shirali, S.; Hu, J.-R.; Nicholas, S. B.; Tuot, D. S.; Errett, N. A.; Lamprea-Montealegre, J. A.
after.abstract: Background: Albuminuria testing to diagnose chronic kidney disease (CKD) and guide blood pressure management is recommended for adults with hypertension but remains underused in part due to suboptimal patient understanding of its importance. Patient facing behavioral interventions have the potential to bridge this gap. We developed and evaluated KnowCKD, a behaviorally informed intervention designed to increase patient awareness of CKD and knowledge and promote albuminuria testing among adults with hypertension. Methods: KnowCKD consisted of an educational infographic and brief, behaviorally informed messages delivered to patients' smartphones during the 5 days leading up to and including a scheduled primary care visit at one academic medical center. Among 57 adults with hypertension without diabetes or recent albuminuria testing, we assessed changes in CKD awareness and knowledge and patient-reported engagement via survey pre- and post- exposure to KnowCKD. Electronic Health Record (EHR)- confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing was compared with 182 contemporaneous primary care controls using unmatched and propensity score-matched analysis. A postintervention focus group evaluated participant experiences. Results: After exposure to KnowCKD, recognition that adults with hypertension should undergo urine testing increased from 58% to 95%, knowledge that albuminuria indicates protein in the urine increased from 47% to 95%, and awareness that testing facilitates early CKD detection increased from 55% to 100% (P <0.001 for all). After the primary care visit, 77% of patients reported asking their clinician about urine testing and 65% reported that testing was ordered. EHR-confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing occurred in 36.8% of KnowCKD participants versus 11.0% of controls (risk ratio, 3.35 [95% CI, 1.96-5.73]; absolute risk difference, 25.9 percentage points [95% CI, 12.5- 39.2]). The propensity score-matched risk ratio was 2.93 (95% CI, 1.59-5.42). Participants described KnowCKD as timely, understandable, and actionable and emphasized trusted health-system communication for broader implementation. Conclusions: KnowCKD was associated with increased patient awareness of CKD and knowledge, patient engagement, and higher EHR-confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing among adults with hypertension. A rigorous evaluation of KnowCKD implementation within routine health-system workflows is warranted as a next step.

after.author_corresponding_institution: The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center
after.abstract: Background: Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) is associated with poor outcomes. Risk factors for progressive CRS are not understood in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Objectives: This study aimed to determine the incidence of progressive CRS and risk factors in individuals with CKD. Methods: Adults with CKD in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study excluding those with heart failure (HF) at baseline were included (n = 3,557). We defined progressive CRS as developing HF and end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) within 12 months. ESKD was defined as needing renal replacement therapy or renal transplant. The associations of baseline risk factors with progressive CRS were examined using Cox proportional hazards models. A sensitivity analysis assessed risk factors in those who developed HF before ESKD and vice versa. Results: 161 patients (4.5%) developed progressive CRS. Traditional risk factors [multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios (HR) (95% CI)] associated with progressive CRS in multivariable models included lower education [1.90 (1.28,2.83)], cardiovascular disease [1.53 (1.07,2.18)], lower estimated glomerular filtration rate [0.64 (0.51,0.82)] and higher albumin to creatinine ratio [2.44 (1.98,3.02)]. Novel risk factors associated included higher levels of alkaline phosphatase, brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-?), growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15), hemoglobin A1C, and lower hemoglobin. Risk factors associated with both ESKD before HF and HF before ESKD were kidney dysfunction, albuminuria, and mineral bone disorder (higher alkaline phosphatase and PTH), inflammation (TNF-?), fibrotic factor (GDF-15), and anemia. Diabetes, CVD, systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, HbA1c, and BNP were more strongly associated when HF preceded ESKD. Conclusions: Both traditional risk factors and novel risk factors associated with inflammation, mineral bone disorder, anemia, diabetes control, albuminuria, worse kidney function, and fibrotic factors are associated with progressive CRS in individuals with CKD. Many of these risk factors are modifiable representing potential areas for intervention.

after.authors: Morran, C.; Srinivasan, P.; Andrew, R.; Pow, E. A.; Padovani, L.; Thackray, Y.; Murphy, R.; Zangana, G.; Krupej, S.; I'Anson, M.; Findlay, L.; Millar, J.; Watts, F.; Moni, M.; Reed, M. J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Emergency Medicine Research Group Edinburgh (EMERGE), Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK; Acute Care Edinburgh, Usher Institute, University of Edinburg
after.abstract: Background: Capturing an electrocardiogram (ECG) during transient symptoms remains challenging in emergency department (ED) patients with palpitations. Following the IPED trial, a smartphone-based ambulatory ECG event recorder pathway was integrated into NHS care. We evaluated this service over five years, assessing diagnostic yield, management, one-year outcomes and predictors of cardiac arrhythmia. Methods: Single-centre service evaluation of consecutive patients referred with palpitations to a smartphone-based ambulatory ECG event recorder clinic between 24th July 2019 and 24th July 2024. Patients underwent event-triggered ECG monitoring using the single-lead Kardia Mobile (AliveCor, Inc.) or their own smartwatch with ECG capability. Clinical characteristics, rhythm recordings, investigations, one-year outcomes and management changes were recorded. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of one-year cardiac arrhythmia diagnosis. Results: 1750 patients attended the clinic, mean age 44.3 +/- 16.1 years, 58.2% female. 1176 patients (67.2%) underwent monitoring with a cardiac arrhythmia directly captured in 67 patients (5.7% of monitored), including atrial fibrillation (n=39), supraventricular tachycardia (13), atrial flutter (9), atrial tachycardia (5) and ventricular tachycardia (1). By one year, 84 (7.1%) who underwent monitoring received a cardiac diagnosis with 79.8% (67/84) established directly via clinic monitoring. Across the entire cohort (n=1750), 114 (6.5%) had a cardiac cause at one year, 1472 (84.2%) had non-cardiac aetiology and 1569 (89.1%) were discharged back to primary care. Medication changes were initiated in 106 patients (6.1%). Independent predictors of a one-year cardiac diagnosis were increasing age (aOR 1.04 per 1-year increase), prior atrial fibrillation/flutter (aOR 5.57) and a presenting symptom of irregular beating (aOR 2.65). Conclusion: Our service provides an effective model for evaluating ED patients with palpitations. Over five years the service reliably detected actionable cardiac arrhythmias while safely discharging nearly 90% of patients to primary care. Clinical characteristics may guide patient selection to maximise clinic efficiency.

after.authors: Winfield, B.; McLean, S. A.; Branham, E. M.; Stanley, N.; House, S. L.; Beaudoin, F. L.; Stevens, J. S.; Neylan, T. C.; Clifford, G. D.; Germine, L. T.; Haran, J. P.; Storrow, A. after.abstract: The biological mechanisms governing recovery versus chronicity of adverse posttraumatic neuropsychiatric sequelae (APNS) remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized longitudinal molecular changes among trauma survivors across ten APNS domains, including pain, anxiety, and depression. Recovery across these diverse clinical outcomes was associated with a shared, temporally coordinated transcriptional signature, characterized by early innate immune activation, subsequent homeostatic and wound-healing processes, and later adaptive immune responses. In contrast, chronic APNS trajectories exhibited limited transcriptional remodeling. We derived and externally validated an RNA-based Recovery Score (RRS) capturing the shared molecular response underlying recovery. Higher RRS was associated with greater clinical recovery, elevated peritraumatic cortisol, and lower cumulative stress exposure. Drug-response profiling identified candidate compounds predicted to mimic recovery-associated transcriptional changes. Together, these findings support posttraumatic recovery as an active biological process and identify shared molecular pathways that may be harnessed to prevent multiple adverse posttraumatic outcomes.

after.authors: Ringleb, M.; Trampert, T.; Trampert, T.; Bloch, W.
after.abstract: Background: There is an increasing strain on our healthcare system due to rising numbers of diseases related to chronic stress. One approach to combat these stress-related complaints is health coaching. However, personal health coaching is expensive and time costly, while digital offers can complement the already existing health coaching strategies. Therefore, this study investigates the effects of an AI-supported, digital health and prevention program. Methods: 253 participants were included in the study, with 113 being analyzed eventually. General stress experience and self-efficacy were assessed at baseline (T1), after six weeks (T2), and three months after the interventional phase (T3) via a Numerical Analog Scale (NAS) with values ranging from 0 to 10, the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), and the PsyCap Scale (CPC). Results: A significant time effect was observed for CPC and PSS. CPC increased significantly from T1 to T2 and T3 and remained stable between T2 and T3, while PSS decreased from T1 to T2 and increased again by T3. All pairwise comparisons were significant. There were also significant time effects for self-reported current health status, health literacy, health awareness, and self-efficacy, with values at T3 being higher than at T1 (for health awareness, this was already evident at T2; for self-efficacy, this was additionally evident between T2 and T3), while no time effect was found for motivation. Conclusion: PREVERY seems to be an effective prevention program to increase psychological capital together with self-reported current health status, health awareness, health literacy, and self-efficacy, while at the same time reducing perceived stress.

after.authors: Ramon-Canellas, P.; Vazquez-Bourgon, J.; Crespo-Facorro, B.; Molto, D.; Escarti, M. J.; Gonzalez-Penas, J.; Arango, C.; Gonzalez-Pinto, A. M.; Fananas, L.; Arias, B.; Bobes, J.; Costas, J.; Martorell, L.; Vilella, E.; Santpere, G.; Muntane, G.
after.abstract: Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a highly heritable psychiatric disorder characterised by substantial clinical heterogeneity. While global polygenic scores (gPGS) capture genetic liability to SCZ, their ability to explain clinical variability remains limited. Pathway-stratified polygenic scores (sPGS) offer a biologically informed approach to patient stratification. In this study, common genetic variants were annotated across five neurotransmitter (NT) signalling pathways - acetylcholine (ACh), dopamine, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glutamate (Glu), and serotonin. sPGS adjusted for sex and ancestry principal components, were calculated in two independent cohorts with different available clinical data (N=3,044 and N=645). By clustering top-decile individuals across the five sPGS dimensions, we classified patients into five mutually exclusive patient profiles, which were then evaluated for their associations with Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) symptom dimensions, age at disease onset (AAO), and three-year clinical remission and treatment response. Although gPGS showed no significant association with clinical outcomes, some sPGS-derived profiles captured clinically relevant heterogeneity across cohorts. Patients assigned to the Ach profile exhibited higher overall symptom severity, particularly negative symptoms and general psychopathology. Patients within the Glu profile were characterised by more severe negative symptoms, earlier AAO, reduced three-year remission, and poorer treatment response. Similarly, the GABA risk profile was also associated with three-year remission rates. These findings suggest that NT pathway-specific polygenic profiling may capture clinically relevant variation overlooked by genome-wide approaches. By identifying genetic profiles associated with symptom severity, disease onset, and longitudinal outcomes, this framework could contribute to biologically informed patient stratification and inform future precision psychiatry approaches in SCZ.

We analysed population-level linked school and hospital administrative data for 1.7m pupils (born 2000-2002) who attended state schools in England. We examined differences by racial-ethnic group and gender in rates and timing of AP enrolment and recording patterns of mental health-related provision and hospital contacts among pupils with AP enrolment. Results. A majority (62.4%) of pupils with AP enrolment had recorded mental health need, highest among Mixed White-Black Caribbean pupils (74.0%). Among those in AP, 52.0% of girls with a mental health-related hospital contact had school provision, compared to 67.3% boys. For some racial-ethnic groups, schools appeared less likely to record need evident in hospital records; 17.5% boys and 36.2% girls from Mixed White-Asian backgrounds enrolled in AP had mental health-related hospital contact without school provision. Conclusion. Among pupils enrolled in AP, documented mental health need is high but unevenly recorded across systems, with inequalities by racial-ethnic group and gender.

after.authors: Grandhe, K. K.; Riedel, T. E.
after.abstract: Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) offers a promising alternative to PCR for low-resource settings, but practical barriers remain. For example there is often the need for reliable electricity, precision heating equipment, and cold-chain storage of reagents. Here, we describe a rudimentary but functional platform that integrates (i) a non-electric, chemically driven water bath capable of sustaining LAMP-relevant temperatures and (ii) lyophilized LAMP assays compatible with simple sample inputs such as diluted saliva or oral rinse. We demonstrate successful LAMP amplification under multiple heating configurations, including a thermos-based chemical bath and field-mimicking setups. This work provides proof-of-concept for a low-cost, portable molecular diagnostic workflow that minimizes infrastructure requirements while maintaining analytical performance.

after.abstract: Elevated plasma phosphorylated tau (p-tau) species are proposed as specific biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology but have also been reported in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Their profile across neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases, as well as their discriminatory value when combined with other plasma biomarkers, remain uncertain. We studied 551 participants (ages 40.1 to 87.1 years; 207 women), comprising 506 patients from the Ontario Neurodegenerative Disease Research Initiative (ONDRI) multi-site cohort and 45 amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) PET-negative cognitively unimpaired controls from the Brain-Eye Amyloid Memory study. Ten diagnostic groups were studied: mild cognitive impairment (MCI), AD, Parkinson's disease subdivided into cognitively unimpaired (CU), MCI, and dementia, frontotemporal dementia (FTD), cerebrovascular disease (CVD) subdivided into cognitively unimpaired (CU) and cognitively impaired (CI), ALS, and the control group. Baseline visit plasma measurements included p-tau217, p-tau181, A{beta}42/40, neurofilament light chain (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). Cross-sectional analyses compared biomarker levels as well as p-tau217-based inference of amyloid positivity status across diagnostic groups. Receiver operating characteristic-area under the curve (ROC-AUC) analyses ascertained the discriminatory capacity of these biomarkers and ratio combinations. Within the ALS group, baseline biomarker measures were also tested for association against baseline clinical features as well as longitudinal measures of neuropsychological change. P-tau217, p-tau181, GFAP, and NfL differed across groups (all P < 0.001). Compared to controls, p-tau217 was elevated in AD and ALS, p-tau181 and GFAP only in AD, and NfL in ALS and FTD. Inferred amyloid-{beta}; positivity was more probable in MCI, AD, ALS, and cognitively impaired CVD groups compared to controls (all P < 0.05). The p-tau217 to NfL ratio discriminated ALS from AD with an ROC-AUC of 0.92 (95% CI 0.85-0.97) compared to p-tau217 alone at 0.65 (95% CI 0.52-0.76). No ALS clinical or longitudinal association survived correction for multiple comparisons. Elevated p-tau217 and inferred amyloid-{beta}; positivity in ALS provide further evidence that the assay signal is not necessarily specific for AD pathology. However, the use of p-tau217 in combination with NfL provides improved discriminatory power between ALS and AD, supporting the use of plasma biomarker combinations rather than sole reliance on individual plasma biomarkers. Inferred amyloid-{beta}; positivity in cognitively impaired CVD may indicate AD and/or cerebral amyloid angiopathy co-pathology. Currently available plasma biomarkers should therefore be used as diagnostic complements and interpreted within clinical context rather than as standalone molecular diagnoses.

after.abstract: Background Autonomic symptoms are common in Parkinson disease (PD) and impact quality of life, with unclear relationship to motor and cognitive progression. Objective: Characterize five-year progression of autonomic symptoms in early PD and their association with motor and cognitive outcomes. Methods We analyzed data from 874 PD participants and 252 healthy controls (HC) enrolled in Parkinson Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). Autonomic symptoms were assessed annually over five years using Scales for Outcomes in Parkinson's disease-Autonomic dysfunction (SCOPA-AUT); affected autonomic domains were defined as domain subscore >1. Clinical measures included MDS-UPDRS and Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Generalized estimating equations evaluated longitudinal changes, adjusting for age, sex, medication, and comorbidities. Results: At baseline, 71% of PD participants reported >1 affected autonomic domain, increasing to 85% among 287 PD participants with 5-year follow-up; HCs reporting >1 affected autonomic domain increased from 40% of participants at baseline to 46% among 145 participants with 5-year follow-up. Gastrointestinal and urinary symptoms were most prevalent in PD. Medication use for constipation and urinary dysfunction increased over time in PD. Cardiovascular comorbidities were common and increased in prevalence in both groups. Greater baseline autonomic symptom burden predicted more rapid cognitive, but not motor decline in PD (p=0.002). Conclusion: Autonomic symptoms in PD are common at disease onset, near universal after 5 years, and associated with faster cognitive, but not motor, decline, driven by those with severe symptoms. The high prevalence and impact of autonomic symptoms in early PD highlights the importance of early assessment and management of these symptoms.

after.abstract: Background. Donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine are dispensed free of charge to people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease in the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS), but their comparative long-term effectiveness in routine care is unknown. Under the national clinical protocol, memantine is added to a cholinesterase inhibitor (ChEI) when the disease reaches the moderate stage, so memantine add-on can serve as a marker of clinical progression. Methods. Nationwide new-user cohort study emulating a target trial in which adults with Alzheimer's disease eligible for a ChEI would be randomly assigned to start donepezil, galantamine or rivastigmine and followed for memantine add-on. We used outpatient medication dispensing authorizations (APAC records of the Outpatient Information System, SIA/SUS) from all 27 federative units, January 2018 to December 2025. We included patients who started a single ChEI between October 2019, after memantine was first recorded nationally, and December 2025, after at least 12 months without anti-dementia dispensing. The outcome was the first memantine dispensing after the index month. Follow-up ended at add-on, recorded death, loss to follow-up (more than 3 observed months without dispensing) or end of data. Deaths were rarely recorded and were treated as censoring. One pseudonymized health card number shared by many patients was excluded, and follow-up ended earlier in the two affected states. We estimated the risk of add-on at 12 to 48 months had all patients started each drug and remained under observation, using stabilized inverse probability of treatment and censoring weights, with 95% confidence intervals (CI) from 200 bootstrap replicates. The analysis assumed no unmeasured confounding or informative censoring given the measured covariates. Results. The cohort included 142 758 new users (donepezil 74 165; galantamine 30 691; rivastigmine 37 902; mean age 77.3 years; 63.0% women), followed for a median of 14 months; 9 812 memantine add-on events occurred. After weighting, all standardized mean differences were below 0.05. The 24-month weighted cumulative incidence of memantine add-on was 9.7% (95% CI 9.4-10.0) with donepezil, 9.0% (8.6-9.4) with galantamine and 5.6% (5.3-5.9) with rivastigmine. Compared with donepezil, the 24-month risk difference was -0.7 percentage points (pp) (-1.1 to -0.3) for galantamine and -4.1 pp (-4.5 to -3.7) for rivastigmine (risk ratio 0.58, 0.55-0.61). Estimates were stable across sensitivity analyses, including a composite outcome that counted unrecorded deaths and dropouts as events (24-month risk difference -4.1 pp, -4.8 to -3.3) and analyses within age groups (risk ratio 0.64 below 75 years). Deaths were almost never recorded in the dispensing data (at most 0.47% of treated patients per year). Conclusions. In routine SUS care, initiation with rivastigmine, mostly as a transdermal patch, was associated with a lower risk of memantine add-on than initiation with donepezil or galantamine. Because disease severity and death are not recorded in the dispensing data, this difference may reflect prescribing patterns or residual confounding by severity rather than slower progression; additional analyses made differential mortality a less likely explanation. It should be confirmed with linked clinical and mortality data.

after.authors: Badjo, J.-P.; Choa, F.-S.
after.abstract: Sensory gating (SG), most commonly quantified using the auditory P50 event-related potential elicited by a paired "double-click" paradigm, is a well-established biomarker of early sensory inhibition that reflects the brain's ability to suppress responses to repetitive sensory input. Although auditory SG paradigms have been widely used in both research and clinical settings, they impose an unavoidable auditory load and are generally limited to controlled laboratory environments, reducing their suitability for ecological monitoring and applications in which auditory resources must remain available. This study evaluated the feasibility of a portable vibrotactile sensory-gating system designed to assess inhibitory processing without engaging the auditory or visual modalities. Fifteen healthy adult participants completed both auditory and vibrotactile paired-stimulus conditions using a within-subject experimental design. Vibrotactile stimuli were delivered through transducers positioned on the volar surface of the forearm while electroencephalographic (EEG) activity was recorded using a 32-channel Emotiv EPOC Flex system. Event-related responses were extracted and analyzed using conventional sensory-gating metrics to enable direct comparison between modalities. Vibrotactile stimulation elicited time-locked P50 responses with attenuation of S2 relative to S1. Mean S2/S1 ratios were 0.521 +- 0.041 for the auditory condition and 0.524 +- 0.064 for the vibrotactile condition. The paired difference was 0.0029 (95% CI, -0.0221 to 0.0279), t(14) = 0.249, p = 0.807, dz = 0.064. No statistically significant difference was detected between modalities in this sample. These group-level findings support further evaluation of portable vibrotactile P50 measurement.

after.abstract: Background: Brain metastases (BMs), the most common intracranial tumor, do not distribute uniformly throughout the brain, but instead preferentially localize to specific regions. Building on known associations with perfusion and the gray-white matter junction, we hypothesized that regional vulnerability to BMs also reflects the cellular and molecular organization of the healthy brain. Methods: In a discovery cohort of 1,406 patients, we generated a voxelwise map of BM distribution and compared it with normative atlases of brain microstructure, vasculature, metabolism, cell-type composition, and gene expression. Associations were tested for replication in an independent multicenter validation cohort of 1,209 patients. Results: In the discovery cohort, BM frequency was higher near the gray-white matter junction and in regions with greater cerebral perfusion, glucose metabolism, and mitochondrial density. At the cellular level, BM frequency was inversely related to astrocyte and microglial transcriptional signatures. Using normative gene expression maps derived from postmortem healthy brain tissue, we identified 17 genes spatially associated with BM vulnerability and specific to metastases relative to other intracranial lesion types. These associations replicated in the validation cohort. The immune checkpoint gene LAG3 ranked among the ten genes most positively associated with metastatic vulnerability across all genes tested (r = 0.40-0.45, p < 0.001). LAG3 expression was also elevated in peritumoral brain metastasis tissue relative to control brain tissue in an independent spatial transcriptomic dataset. Conclusions: These findings suggest that BM vulnerability reflects healthy brain organization and identify LAG-3, a clinically targetable immune checkpoint, as a candidate link between regional brain immune biology and metastatic colonization.

The EpiDirect technology represents a novel analytical approach that enables direct, quantitative assessment of DNA methylation by qPCR using native, unmodified DNA. Here we compared the EpiDirect MGMT Methylation qPCR Assay to MGMTp pyrosequencing using brain tumor samples to evaluate the correlation between the two methods. after.authors: Garcia, C.; Guerit, F.; Arzounian, D.; Carlyon, R. P.
after.abstract: Purpose: We investigated the mechanisms behind the generation of Neural Distortion Responses (NDRs) measured with electroencephalography when interleaving amplitude-modulated (AM) pulse trains in cochlear implant (CI) users. Methods: Previous experiments measured NDRs using interleaved pulse trains in which odd- and even-numbered pulses were respectively modulated at F1 and F2 Hz, where F1=2*F2/3 and F1{approx}80Hz. Experiment 1 separated quadratic and cubic distortion products using a relationship of F1 and F2 such that F1 = (2*F2/3)+2. Experiment 2 retained the original F1=2*F2/3 relationship but shifted the starting AM phase of F2 relative to that of F1. Experiment 3 simultaneously separated the quadratic and cubic distortion products and varied the relative phase of F1 and F2. Experiment 4 flipped the leading polarity of the second pulse in each pulse-pair such that the central phase of the resulting pseudo-triphasic pulses was anodic. All experiments were conducted with Cochlear CI users and interpreted using two computational models of the electrically stimulated auditory nerve. Results: Both quadratic (QDR) and cubic distortion products (CDR) were observed. Varying relative AM phase had an effect on NDR amplitudes, with the largest amplitude when maxima of the 2 AM patterns were aligned. Stimulating with an anodic central phase within the AM pulse pairs resulted in stronger responses for 4 of 9 CI users. Computational modelling suggested a stronger role for refractoriness than for facilitation in generating the NDR, but failed to fully account for the effect of flipping the polarity. Conclusion: NDRs consist of both quadratic and cubic components, and are greatest when maxima of the F1 and F2 pulse trains align. Refractoriness is likely more important than facilitation for generating the NDR.

after.title: Preprint: Polygenic Prediction of Depression Liability Reveals Broad Genetic Associations Across Development, Families, and Populations
after.authors: Wolfram, T.; Moore, S. M.; Anomaly, J.; Schleede, J.; Ahangari, M.
after.abstract: Polygenic prediction of depression is limited by the depth of depression phenotyping available at biobank scale as well as sample size. Here we develop a depression score combining information from depression and genetically correlated psychiatric traits using phenotype reconstruction, multi-trait genetic integration and Bayesian effect estimation. Compared with the strongest publicly available depression-only score (Psychiatric Genomics Consortium 2025, excluding 23andMe), the liability-R2 for depression in UK Biobank rose by 49.7% and within-family standardized associations with latent internalizing were up to 54% larger. Across 2,328 childhood and adolescent outcomes in the ABCD study, the association profile of the integrated score was almost identical to that of the depression-only score (r = 0.99), while being uniformly stronger. 1,494 outcomes related to mood, behavior, social functioning, hobbies and sleep were associated with the score -- 423 of them within-family. In ABCD, adolescents in the highest score decile were 3.5 times as likely as those in the lowest decile to report suicidal thoughts by age 14 (23% versus 7%) and 1.9 times as likely to report nicotine or cannabis use by age 17 (47% versus 25%). In adults, the score predicted worse general health, chronic pain, and life dissatisfaction. Associations with psychiatric symptoms were substantially stronger in girls than in boys (boys' coefficients 0.68 times girls'), particularly for girl-typical symptoms, and showed no moderation by household resources, hardship or deprivation that remained significant after correction for multiple testing. Prediction was attenuated in line with genetic distance from training data for Hispanic and African American children. Depression prediction can thus be strengthened substantially by integrating the internalizing spectrum, without detectable loss of specificity or within-family predictive ability.

after.authors: Pilli, K.; Allan, T. J.; Bennett, M. F.; Harris, R. V.; Schneider, A. L.; Shen, Q.; Ma, J. G.; Hildebrand, M. S.; Palmer, E. E.; George, A. L.; Berkovic, S. F.; Vandenberg, J. I.; Scheffer, I. E.; Ng, C.-A.
after.abstract: SCN1A, the most prominent gene for epilepsy, encodes the pore-forming subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel, NaV1.1. Loss-of-function variants reduce NaV1.1 activity in inhibitory neurons leading to hyperexcitability; they are associated with a spectrum of epilepsies, from self-limited phenotypes in genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus, to the prototypic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, Dravet syndrome. Thousands of SCN1A missense variants have been identified, but determining pathogenicity using ACMG criteria can be challenging. Currently, 48% of missense SCN1A variants in ClinVar are classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS). We aimed to provide functional evidence to inform variant classification using a high-throughput automated patch-clamp assay. We validated our assay using 27 true pathogenic SCN1A variants and 25 true benign variants. The results show that 17/27 true pathogenic variants from patients with Dravet syndrome showed severe reductions in current density, precluding gating analysis. Of the remaining ten true pathogenic variants, seven showed an increased voltage difference between the midpoints of activation and inactivation (V0.5diff). Current density and V0.5diff were combined within a graded Bayesian framework to derive a functional log-likelihood ratio reflecting the magnitude of loss of function. We then applied our validated assay to 16 SCN1A missense variants detected in an Australian cohort: three likely pathogenic, one likely benign and 12 VUSs. These variants occurred in 31 individuals from 16 families with a broad phenotypic spectrum, including four individuals with Dravet syndrome who carried p.Ser243Phe, p.Met973Val or p.Lys1911Glu. All three variants showed loss of function: p.Ser243Phe had reduced current density, whereas p.Met973Val and p.Lys1911Glu had abnormal V0.5diff despite current density within the normal range. Of these 16 variants, ten have combined functional scores consistent with abnormal functional evidence. Combining our functional evidence with ACMG criteria, our findings changed the classification of eight of 16 variants (50%), with six of 12 VUS reclassified as likely pathogenic and two of three likely pathogenic variants upgraded to pathogenic. We show that calibrated automated patch-clamp assays can provide actionable functional data to enable the interpretation and reclassification of SCN1A variants and inform clinical care, allowing therapeutic optimisation and facilitating access to genetic therapies.

after.authors: Keating, N.; Mesdaghi, M.; Chavoshzadeh, Z.; Karimi, A.; Saberi, M.; Unal, S.; Meynier, V.; Soudee, C.; Laine, C.; Solgi, A.; Sharafian, S.; LHonneur, A.-S.; Migaud, M.; Seeleuthner, Y.; Cobat, A.; Abel, L.; Beziat, V.; Rosain, J.; Bustamante, J.; Casanova, J.-L.; Boisson-Dupuis, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center
after.abstract: Two otherwise healthy patients from Colombia, now aged 30 and 38 years, developed pulmonary tuberculosis due to inherited, complete TNF deficiency at the ages of 19 and 18 years. We report here a previously healthy Iranian patient with inherited complete TNF deficiency who was diagnosed with both pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB between 10 and 15 years of age. The homozygous TNF variant (c.673C>T) introduces a premature stop codon (TNF p.Q225*) resulting in losses of expression and function. Despite normal myeloid and lymphoid subset development, the patient's primary leukocytes do not secrete detectable amounts of TNF. As in the TNF-deficient Colombian patients, the respiratory burst of GM-CSF-derived macrophages is impaired. Our findings expand the spectrum of TB phenotypes in patients with TNF deficiency and confirm that TNF is essential for immunity to M. tuberculosis in humans but apparently redundant against many other pathogens, including weakly virulent mycobacteria.

after.authors: Tran, H.; Mulford, A. J.; Wei, J.; Shi, Z.; Ashworth, A.; Zheng, S. L.; Helfand, B. T.; Hulick, P. J.; DePersia, A.; Suh, G.; Jones, B.; Sanders, A. R.; Xu, J.
after.abstract: Background: Published colorectal cancer (CRC) polygenic risk scores (PRS) may demonstrate similar population-level predictive performance but often assign substantially different risk classifications to the same individuals. Such discordance presents challenges for clinical implementation and return of results (RoR). Methods: We developed a stable PRS for CRC (stPRS-CRC) by integrating 28 published PRS using PRSmix in the All of Us (AoU) development cohort (n=321,703). Performance was evaluated in a held-out AoU validation cohort (n=80,423) and independently validated in the Genomic Health Initiative (GHI) (n=17,545). CRC associations were assessed using logistic regression, comparing individuals in the highest PRS decile with the remaining 90%. Individual-level concordance in high-risk classification was evaluated using mean Jaccard indices. Results: Published CRC PRS showed substantial discordance in individual-level high-risk classification despite generally consistent associations with CRC. stPRS-CRC integrated information from multiple published PRS and demonstrated CRC associations comparable to PGS003852, the strongest-performing individual PRS. The odds ratios for stPRS-CRC were 1.94 (95% CI, 1.79-2.11) in AoU development, 2.08 (1.76-2.45) in AoU validation, and 2.08 (1.55-2.79) in GHI. Mean Jaccard indices using stPRS-CRC versus PGS003852 as anchors, each compared with the same 27 published PRS, were 0.29 versus 0.20, 0.43 versus 0.25, and 0.27 versus 0.19, respectively (all P<0.001). Conclusions: Integrating multiple published CRC PRS significantly improved individual-level concordance in high-risk classification while maintaining population-level predictive performance. stPRS-CRC may provide a more consistent framework for clinical genetic risk assessment and ROR.

after.authors: Clapp Sullivan, M. L.; de la Fuente, J.; Corley, J.; Harris, S. E.; Deary, I. J.; Russ, T. C.; Cox, S. R.; Tucker-Drob, E. M.
after.abstract: Alzheimers disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) are clinical disorders characterized by declines in cognitive function to levels at which everyday living is meaningfully impaired. Genetic variants may confer risk for AD/ADRD by way of steeper rates of aging-related cognitive declines or their association with lower premorbid levels of cognitive function that place individuals closer to a clinically severe threshold of cognitive function. We applied joint longitudinal-hazard models to 26-year data from an ancestrally diverse US sample of N = 11,518 adults to estimate effects of multi-ancestry polygenic indices (PGIs) for a range of established risk factors on dementia hazard and the degree they operate via premorbid cognitive function and longitudinal cognitive decline. APOE e4 and PGIs for ADRD, type 2 diabetes, stroke, LDL cholesterol, and hearing loss operated via rate of change, whereas PGIs for educational attainment, cognitive function, physical activity, BMI, smoking, loneliness, schizophrenia, and externalizing were associated with dementia hazard via premorbid differences in cognitive function. Some results varied by continental ancestry. Our implementation of joint longitudinal-hazard models allowed us to distinguish how different genetic risk factors for AD/ADRD operate via degenerative processes that might be therapeutically targeted during later life and via premorbid levels of cognitive function that would require intervention earlier in the life course.

after.abstract: BACKGROUND: Many transfusion reactions are not reported to hemovigilance systems, and the features needed to recognize them are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. We sought to develop and evaluate an open-source, multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline to extract transfusion reaction features defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Hemovigilance Module from clinical notes. METHODS: We curated 181 features from the NHSN protocol and developed a multi-stage pipeline that extracted features, their timing, and clinical details from free-text notes. Three open-weight large language models (Qwen 3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Kimi K3) were applied to 50 notes from expert-written scenarios, published case reports, and MIMIC-IV discharge summaries. Two physicians independently evaluated every model output in a blinded interface. The primary analysis was restricted to feature occurrences with concordant physician assessments. RESULTS: Physicians agreed on 1,201 of 1,343 co-rated feature occurrences (89.4%; Krippendorff's alpha 0.73). Precision was above 0.98 for all models. Sensitivity was 0.774 (95% CI 0.745-0.800) for Kimi K3, 0.636 (0.604-0.667) for GPT-OSS-120B, and 0.624 (0.593-0.655) for Qwen 3.6-27B, and specificity ranged from 0.952 to 0.991. Omissions accounted for more than 94% of false negatives. Timing and clinical details were judged supported or reasonable in more than 92% and 97% of assessments, respectively. Results were consistent across note sources and in analyses including discordant assessments. CONCLUSION: Multi-agent AI pipelines provide a feasible method for extracting transfusion reaction signals from clinical notes with high precision. Our work may have applications in active hemovigilance, reaction classification, and big data research.
after.summary: BACKGROUND: Many transfusion reactions are not reported to hemovigilance systems, and the features needed to recognize them are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. We sought to develop and evaluate an open-source, multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline to extract transfusion reaction features defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Hemovigilance Module from clinical notes. METHODS: We curated 181 features from the NHSN protocol and developed a multi-stage pipeline that extracted features, their timing, and clinical details from free-text notes. Three open-weight large language models (Qwen 3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Kimi K3) were applied to 50 notes from expert-written scenarios, published case reports, and MIMIC-IV discharge summaries. Two physicians independently evaluated every model output in a blinded interface. The primary analysis was restricted to feature occurrences with concordant physician assessments. RESULTS: Physicians agreed on 1,201 of 1,343 co-rated feature occurrences (89.4%; Krippendorff's alpha 0.73). Precision was above 0.98 for all models. Sensitivity was 0.774 (95% CI 0.745-0.800) for Kimi K3, 0.636 (0.604-0.667) for GPT-OSS-120B, and 0.624 (0.593-0.655) for Qwen 3.6-27B, and specificity ranged from 0.952 to 0.991. Omissions accounted for more than 94% of false negatives. Timing and clinical details were judged supported or reasonable in more than 92% and 97% of assessments, respectively. Results were consistent across note sources and in analyses including discordant assessments. CONCLUSION: Multi-agent AI pipelines provide a feasible method for extracting transfusion reaction signals from clinical notes with high precision. Our work may have applications in active hemovigilance, reaction classification, and big data research.

after.authors: Honerlaw, J.; MacArthur, J. A. L.; Ho, Y.-L.; Gangireddy, S.; Galloway, A.; Hilty, K.; Rao, G.; Li, L.; Shoaibi, A.; Denaxas, S.; Cho, K.; Wei, W.-Q.
after.abstract: Objective: To identify community - prioritized metadata for reporting and sharing computable phenotypes (CPs), develop a cross-library candidate framework, assess alignment between user requirements and library metadata, and test the feasibility of metadata exchange. Materials and Methods: We combined an international, library - led effort by the Open PhEnomics Network (OPEN) consortium with a UK community consensus-building exercise aimed at improving the FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) of CPs. The consortium performed a cross-library field comparison and literature review to inform candidate fields, refined through consortium consensus. The community approach was developed through stakeholder interviews, a survey, and workshop, guided by a working group. Community requirements were interpretively mapped to the resulting framework and classified into conformance tiers. Interoperability was tested by manually and programmatically mapping diabetes-related phenotypes across libraries. Results: The library - led process produced 23 candidate fields spanning phenotype description, data/technical details, and performance domains. Thirteen fields aligned across all five libraries, and 22 fields aligned with published CP library desiderata. Interoperability testing successfully catalogued phenotypes through manual mapping, with API - mediated mapping achieving 63 - 76% metadata field completeness across libraries. A community survey (n=124 respondents) identified six metadata elements with majority support as mandatory: description, coding terminology, phenotype type, version history, unique identifier, and data source. Logic representation and validation requirements were rated as mostly context-dependent. Community - identified priorities showed strong alignment with the OPEN framework, though some requirements were only partially represented. Discussion: Through a consensus - based, community - driven approach, we established a CP framework enabling interoperability across libraries. Conclusion: OPEN provides a credible, community - informed foundation for a FAIR CP metadata standard.

after.title: Preprint: Twenty-five years of phage therapy funding: rapid growth, narrow base
after.authors: Mbogning Fonkou, M. D.; Yanwou, N.; Bamou, R.; Tsayem Ngueguim, I.; YACOUBA, A.
after.abstract: Background. Bacteriophage therapy is moving from compassionate use toward regulated clinical use, as antimicrobial resistance (AMR) grows. Who pays for phage therapy research, and where the money goes, has not been measured globally. Methods. We searched Dimensions on 13 February 2024 and screened 1,521 grant records. We analysed the 802 grants with a recorded funding amount that started in 1999-2023 (USD 318.6 million). We estimated log-linear growth, measured concentration with the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) and Gini coefficient, and counted shared grants fractionally across recipient institutions. Topics came from latent Dirichlet allocation, and team gender from first names. Sensitivity analyses added the 272 relevant grants without an amount, merged yearly records into projects, and varied key definitions. Results. Grants grew by 12.2% a year and recorded funding by 16.6% a year (14.1% after inflation), yet the field received only about USD 13 million a year. US funders provided 47.7% of funding and one institute, NIAID, 21.0%, rising to 23.3% in 2016-2023. The top 10% of recipient institutions received 53.4%. Low- and lower-middle-income countries received 0.33% of recorded funding, and only 7 grants linked Global North and Global South recipients. Antibiotic-resistance research rose from 3% to about a quarter of funding. Female-only teams received grants 19% smaller than male-only teams after adjustment (95% CI -32 to -2), and 84% of researchers held a single grant. Counting grants rather than dollars, the Global South received 17.5%, because several of its funders report no amounts. The headline results held in 37 of 40 sensitivity checks. Conclusions. Phage therapy research funding is growing fast from a small base, but it rests on a narrow set of funders and countries and rarely reaches the countries most affected by AMR. Broader funding, and fuller reporting of national investments, will matter as phage therapy enters regulated clinical use. https://cognosx.ca/dashboards/phage-funding.html

after.abstract: The human microbiome is critical for health across the life course and may mediate the relationship between early-life exposures and health outcomes. The Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (ECHO) Cohort provides a unique opportunity to investigate this relationship in children. Individual cohort sites within the ECHO Cohort collected and sequenced microbiome data prior to the consortium formation. Sequencing data were annotated using a common protocol. We summarized the relationship between participant characteristics and features of the microbiome to understand how ECHO can advance the study of the connection between environmental exposures, the microbiome, and health outcomes. A total of 15,509 high-quality extant microbiome samples were collected from 1,086 pregnancies and 5,701 children from 21 ECHO cohort sites. The observed microbial communities were shaped by body site, participant type (pregnant person, child), age, and sample processing. Children lived in 40 states across the United States; high-quality geolocation data were available for more than 60% of children with gut samples. Assay measures, including PFAS, and were available for more than 1,000 children with gut samples. Extant ECHO microbiome data provide an opportunity to characterize the effect of environmental exposures on the developing human microbiome and the role of these exposures in shaping long-term health.

after.title: Preprint: Relationship between Excess Mortality Derived from Death Counts and Age-Standardised Mortality Rates: The Case of Germany During the COVID-19 Pandemic
after.authors: Sauter, M.
after.abstract: Excess mortality can be estimated from crude death counts or from age-standardised mortality rates (ASMRs). Although both approaches are widely used, their analytical relationship and the effects of methodological choices such as standard population, age-group definition, and baseline selection are not always explicitly considered. The analytical relationship between relative excess mortality based on death counts and ASMRs was derived and both approaches were applied to mortality in Germany during the COVID19 pandemic 2020-2023. Expected mortality was estimated by linear extrapolation of pre-pandemic trends. ASMR calculations were repeated using different standard populations, age-group definitions, open-ended age groups, and reference periods. Death-count- and ASMR-based P-scores were analytically equivalent when the age distribution of the standard population corresponded to that of the population under study. Empirically, both approaches yielded closely corresponding estimates for Germany. The effect of the standard population depended on the age distribution of excess mortality and was particularly pronounced in 2020, when excess mortality was concentrated at older ages. The definition of the open-ended age group had an additional effect: aggregating ages 80+ altered the pre-pandemic ASMR trend, and consequently changed the estimated excess mortality. Variation of the pre-pandemic reference period substantially affected P-scores, but death-count- and ASMR-based estimates changed in a closely corresponding manner. Relative excess mortality derived from death counts and ASMRs is closely related, and differences between the approaches can be explained by their underlying weighting and baseline assumptions. For trend-based excess mortality estimation, the standard population, age-group definition, and baseline specification are therefore integral methodological choices. Death counts provide a simple and transparent reference measure for analyses within a single population, whereas age-standardised estimates require careful consideration of these additional assumptions.

after.authors: Kim, C.; McConnell, E. V.; Schumacher, S. G.; Falzon, D.; Gegia, M.; Aprilawati, L.; Galarza, J.; Tembo, E.; Tonkonoh, L.; Knight, G. M.; McQuaid, C. F.; Mirzayev, F.; West, N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
after.abstract: Objective: To assess stakeholder acceptability of and preferences for long-acting injectables (LAIs) for tuberculosis (TB) treatment and prevention across World Health Organization regions to inform product development and implementation. Methods: We conducted a sequential explanatory mixed-methods study of survey data and qualitative focus group discussions (FGDs). Online surveys assessed perceptions and acceptance of LAIs among two groups: TB programme managers, civil society members and healthcare workers (Survey A), and community members and persons affected by TB (Survey B). Using purposive sampling, survey participants were invited to join FGDs to explore survey findings. Survey data were analysed using descriptive statistics, ordinal logistic regression with stepwise AIC selection, and one-sample proportion tests. FGD transcripts were analysed using modified framework analysis. Findings: Among 310 participants (102 Survey A; 208 Survey B), 83% (n=256) favoured LAIs over standard oral TB treatment. Compared with six months of daily oral treatment, 69% preferred a three-month regimen comprising one month of daily oral treatment followed by four injections per monthly visit for two months, while 80% preferred the corresponding regimen with two injections per visit. For prevention, 79% preferred a single injection over one month of oral treatment. In Survey B, interest varied according to lived TB experience, with FGDs suggesting that previous negative experiences with injectables may have contributed to this variation. Conclusion: Interest in LAIs for TB treatment and prevention was high, but lower among participants with lived TB experience. Product development and implementation should address concerns about injectables and side effects while preserving patient choice and agency.

after.abstract: Introduction Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is one of the leading causes of global disability and disability-adjusted life years. One of the key systemic features of COPD is impaired skeletal muscle mass and function, termed sarcopenia. The recognition of skeletal muscle dysfunction as a treatable trait in COPD opens a therapeutic avenue for pharmacological development, with the aim of improving physical function and reducing healthcare utilisation. A novel combination drug, RJx-01, was identified as a candidate therapy for sarcopenia based on preclinical evidence. The primary aim of this study is to evaluate the safety and tolerability of RJx-01 compared with placebo following hospitalisation with an acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD), when acute deterioration of skeletal muscle integrity is observed. Exploratory efficacy analyses will assess differences in muscle function, mass, and multi-omic-derived outcomes. Methods and analysis The MINT-COPD trial is a phase IIa, single centre, randomised controlled trial (RCT). Eighty participants admitted to hospital with AECOPD will be randomly assigned 1:1 to receive either oral RJx-01 or placebo, once daily for 24 weeks. The primary outcome is safety and tolerability of RJx-01 compared with placebo in COPD patients. Exploratory objectives aim to assess the preliminary effects of AECOPD-associated hospitalisation and RJx-01 treatment on muscle mass, function, and fatiguability, as well as patient reported symptoms and frailty. The optional skeletal muscle biopsy sub-study aims to assess the effects of AECOPD on proteomic and transcriptomic markers of skeletal muscle.

after.authors: Hum, R. M.; Christofi, M.; Smith, S. L.; Tan, Y.; Shukla, R.; Marshall, L. M.; Smith, M.; Williams, A.; Orozco, G.; Viatte, S.; Buch, M.; Barton, A.; Ho, P.; Martin, P.
after.abstract: Background Synovial inflammation in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) lacks a validated histological classification framework. Current approaches apply rheumatoid arthritis (RA) synovial pathotypes to PsA, which overlooks immunobiological differences between the diseases and limits the predictive power of tissue stratification. We aimed to define data-driven, PsA-specific synovial pathotypes to facilitate tissue-driven precision medicine. Methods In this cross-sectional study, ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies were obtained from 61 patients with PsA (n=22), seropositive RA (n=23), seronegative RA (n=10), and other inflammatory arthritides (n=6). Sections underwent multi-modal staining, including H&E, picrosirius red, and immunohistochemistry for CD3, CD20, CD68, CD138, and CD31. Whole-slide digital image analysis and automated pixel classifiers quantified cellular and stromal metrics. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering identified intrinsic PsA pathotypes, which were correlated with clinical disease activity, radiographic osteoarthritis (OA), and longitudinal treatment responses. Findings While a subset of PsA patients shared an inflammatory signature with seropositive RA, unsupervised clustering of the PsA cohort revealed three distinct, novel pathotypes: Dense Myeloid (macrophage-driven), Fibro-Stromal (fibrosis and pauci-immune), and Angio-Lymphoid (hypervascular with significant CD138+ plasma cell infiltration). Pathotypes were independent of treatment and concurrent radiographic knee OA. The Fibro-Stromal pathotype correlated with significantly higher cutaneous psoriasis severity. Longitudinally, patients with the Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited a trend toward lower treatment response (44%) following standard interventions (methotrexate or TNF inhibitors) compared to the Dense Myeloid (50%) and Angio-Lymphoid (80%) pathotypes. Interpretation We present the first computationally derived synovial pathotypes specific to PsA, revealing distinct plasma cell and fibrotic architectures not captured by RA-centric models. To enable clinical translation, we distilled these findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree (CD31, CD68, CD138, and picrosirius red) designed for routine histopathology workflows, providing a staging ground for biomarker-stratified clinical trials in PsA. Funding Funding from the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Manchester, Arthritis UK, the Wellcome Trust, Brit-PACT, the National Psoriasis Foundation, and the Medical Research Council.

Methods In this cross-sectional study, ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies were obtained from 61 patients with PsA (n=22), seropositive RA (n=23), seronegative RA (n=10), and other inflammatory arthritides (n=6). Sections underwent multi-modal staining, including H&E, picrosirius red, and immunohistochemistry for CD3, CD20, CD68, CD138, and CD31. Whole-slide digital image analysis and automated pixel classifiers quantified cellular and stromal metrics. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering identified intrinsic PsA pathotypes, which were correlated with clinical disease activity, radiographic osteoarthritis (OA), and longitudinal treatment responses. Findings While a subset of PsA patients shared an inflammatory signature with seropositive RA, unsupervised clustering of the PsA cohort revealed three distinct, novel pathotypes: Dense Myeloid (macrophage-driven), Fibro-Stromal (fibrosis and pauci-immune), and Angio-Lymphoid (hypervascular with significant CD138+ plasma cell infiltration). Pathotypes were independent of treatment and concurrent radiographic knee OA. The Fibro-Stromal pathotype correlated with significantly higher cutaneous psoriasis severity. Longitudinally, patients with the Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited a trend toward lower treatment response (44%) following standard interventions (methotrexate or TNF inhibitors) compared to the Dense Myeloid (50%) and Angio-Lymphoid (80%) pathotypes. Interpretation We present the first computationally derived synovial pathotypes specific to PsA, revealing distinct plasma cell and fibrotic architectures not captured by RA-centric models. To enable clinical translation, we distilled these findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree (CD31, CD68, CD138, and picrosirius red) designed for routine histopathology workflows, providing a staging ground for biomarker-stratified clinical trials in PsA. after.abstract: Purpose: This study examined how people living with chronic spinal pain experience, interpret and navigate social representations of their condition and the interactions these generate across clinical, occupational, and personal settings. Materials and Methods: Thirty semi-structured interviews were analysed using an approach informed by constructivist grounded theory, through initial, focused and theoretical coding. Results: Five categories emerged, capturing how social representations and relational dynamics threatened the social self and prompted deliberate strategies for restoring agency. Theoretical coding identified a central process (maintaining and rebuilding the social self), describing how participants navigated these threats across social contexts. Notably, approximately half the participants reproduced, without revision, representations of chronic pain typical of the general population, directing judgements of simulation or inadequate effort at others with the condition. These strategies primarily aimed to restore agency and maintain a viable social self, rather than to reduce pain. Conclusions: These findings describe one process through which social environments shape the experience of chronic spinal pain by influencing how the social self is continually negotiated. Recognising these processes may help rehabilitation professionals attend to the social dimensions of chronic pain.

after.abstract: Rare genetic disorders frequently remain undiagnosed despite the use of exome sequencing (ES) and genome sequencing (GS). This study aimed to enhance diagnostic yield by introducing a systematic framework: SMART filtering (Systematic, Multi-step, Automated, Rare variant prioritization Tool), designed to optimize GS analysis, with a particular emphasis on non-coding regions. We retrospectively analyzed 153 cases with previously negative ES and GS results. SMART filtering was applied as a pre-annotation filtering step, integrating conservation metrics, allele frequency thresholds, and splicing prediction scores. Then followed by phenotype-based prioritization and manual review. Application of this framework identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 4.6% of cases, strong variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in 1.3%, and additional candidate variants in 5.2% of cases. Several deep-intronic variants were confirmed by RNA studies and segregation analyses. The framework enabled efficient prioritization of non-coding and regulatory variants that were overlooked by standard analyses. In conclusion, SMART filtering offers a reproducible and scalable strategy to improve diagnostic yield in GS, particularly in cases where conventional analysis methods fall short. Integrating such frameworks into clinical genomic pipelines can enhance variant interpretability and diagnostic performance, ultimately leading to better patient care outcomes.

after.authors: Rozumek, G. M.; Lim, R. S.; Presley, W.; Blevins, B.; Guan, B.; Han, J. Y. S.; Ullah, E.; Naik, A.; Hahn, T. E.; Young, R.; Moroi, S. E.; Hufnagel, R. B.; Miller, J. M. L.; Prasov, L.
after.abstract: Purpose: Myelin regulatory factor is a transcription factor essential for RPE development and serves as a critical "GO" signal for eye growth. Pathogenic variants in MYRF manifest in a spectrum of clinical phenotypes ranging from isolated nanophthalmos to severe syndromic disease, in a gene dosage dependent manner. In this study, we aimed to determine the pathogenicity and molecular mechanism of a novel variant in the MYRF ICA domain, c.2083C>T (p.R695C), that leads to isolated nanophthalmos and mild retinal pigment epithelial disruption. Methods: Whole genome sequencing was performed and identified a novel MYRF variant. Pathogenecity and in silico modeling were evaluated using the Ensembl VEP tool and PyMOL. Human primary RPE and/or ARPE-19 cells were transduced with FLAG-tagged variant and wildtype MYRF or double-tagged FLAG-MYRF-MYC proteins to evaluate transcriptional activity, localization, and protein trafficking. Results: In silico modeling supports variant pathogenicity and altered homotrimer conformation. Functional studies in human primary RPE (hRPE) and/or ARPE-19 cells confirmed that MYRF p.R695C is cleavage deficient, mislocalized to the apical surface of polarized RPE, and demonstrated reduced synergistic transcriptional activity with co-factor SOX10 in HEK293T cells. Protein trafficking studies demonstrated that wildtype MYRF is trafficked to the apical cell surface and plasma membrane and that endogenous MYRF requires ER to Golgi trafficking pathways for proper nuclear localization and cleavage dynamics. Conclusions: Together, these results confirm that p.R695C is pathogenic for nanophthalmos, implicate trafficking as a regulatory mechanism of MYRF in the hRPE, and support that RPE disruption as a feature of MYRF-associated nanophthalmos.

after.title: Preprint: Accelerometer Data Harmonization and Feature Engineering for Gait Analytics
after.authors: Carrle, F. P.; Schmidt, F.; Reichenbach, A.
after.abstract: Gait analytics is utilized for a wide range of health-related applications, ranging from fitness tracking to medical diagnostics, and beyond. Inertial measurement units that are ubiquitously available in mobile devices provide an accessible means of gait analysis but differences in sensor specifications, placement, and recording protocols limit comparability across studies. This study developed and evaluated an analysis-centered data warehouse and standardized quality-assessed processing pipeline to facilitate the integration and joint analysis of heterogeneous gait accelerometer data. Six publicly available datasets including a total of 935 persons were integrated into a star-schema data warehouse, and feature comparability was assessed across datasets and sensor locations. Gender classification served as a proof-of-concept downstream analysis. Gait-cycle extraction, which serves as foundation for feature extraction, was successfully achieved with an accuracy above 99% for the dataset that provides ground truth information. Comparability varied across datasets and sensor configurations, with correlation coefficients between average gait cycles ranging from 0.5 to close to 1.0. Centrally positioned sensors generally show greater correspondence than peripheral sensors, although differences in statistical features persist even between sensors at nominally identical locations. Gender classification performance remains largely near chance level, and no consistent benefit from pooling datasets could be established. These findings demonstrate that heterogeneous gait accelerometer data can be integrated and processed within a common analytical framework, but standardized processing alone does not ensure comparability of the resulting features. The proposed open-source framework implemented in Python provides a foundation for reproducible cross-study gait analysis and for investigating residual heterogeneity associated with datasets and sensor configurations.

after.title: Preprint: BioLT: Streaming Biosignal Modeling
after.authors: Han, J.; Liu, Y.; Tang, W.; Thwaites, L.; Clifton, D. A.; Gu, X.
after.abstract: Clinical biosignals such as ECG, PPG, and EEG are increasingly acquired as hours-long streams from bedside monitors and wearables, yet existing analysis pipelines almost universally operate on isolated short windows of around 10 seconds and cannot process the long, irregular, frequently interrupted signals. We introduce BioLT, a streaming decoder-only framework for long-context biosignal modeling that turns any window-level feature extractor or pretrained biosignal foundation model into a streaming model. BioLT combines (i) a discontinuity-aware encoding that exposes the inter-window elapsed time as an explicit input channel, so that the decoder can learn to model these gaps as clinically meaningful information, and (ii) a fixed-size compressed memory bank supervised with cumulative summary statistics, which keeps both training and inference linear in the recording length while preserving long-range context. We evaluate on CPSC-2021, VitalDB, MC-MED, and CHB-MIT for arrhythmia, sepsis, and seizure detection and for forecasting up to 20 minutes ahead, using domain features and embeddings from six biosignal foundation models. Across 21 dataset-feature settings, BioLT achieves the highest detection AUROC in 15 and the highest 20-minute forecasting AUROC in 13 settings, and shows consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art snapshot foundation-model embeddings. These highlight the importance of modeling how streaming biosignal representations evolve over time, beyond improving window-level representations alone.

after.title: Preprint: Concern seriousness quantified in regulatory decisions as a main factor in questioning safe, trustworthy medical practice: a cross-sectional study
after.authors: Caballero, J. A.
after.abstract: Background: The main factors related to regulatory decision outcomes reflect the pragmatic expectations of physicians to deliver safe patient care and uphold trust in the profession. Yet empirically understanding critical ones, like concern seriousness, has proven difficult. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we developed a new quantitative measure of concern seriousness via expert focus groups. Using multivariate modelling, we investigated its statistical association with regulatory decisions about all physicians involved in the UK over the 10 years ending with March 2023, within a population of 416,610. Decisions by stage were: whether to investigate complaints; investigation outcomes, including adjudication hearing referral; and hearing outcomes. We controlled for dozens of potential confounders, simultaneously addressing many live questions; giving adjusted odds ratios for associations of outcomes to: criminal conviction, seriousness, allegation types, complaint sources, practice type (e.g. GP, paediatrician, trainee), workplace history, personal characteristics (e.g. age, sex), international/domestic qualification, socioeconomics (e.g. childhood deprivation), exam results (e.g. IELTS), and many more. Results: Severe outcomes predominantly related to factors similar across stages: criminal conviction, high seriousness, allegations of criminality, honesty or fairness, and the complaint coming from the physician's employer, police, or others acting in a professional capacity. Controlling for seriousness chiefly adjusted associations to conviction and allegation types, explaining some away. Conclusions: All else equal, the seriousness of concerns was one of the main factors related to regulatory outcomes. Such main factors underline what is practically expected of physicians to avoid for safe and trustworthy medical practice.

after.title: Preprint: Reducing Biosecurity Risks in Informal Poultry Slaughter: A Pilot Intervention Among Mobile Poultry Vendors in Bangladesh
after.authors: Baker, M. M.; Chowdhury, K. I. A.; Yeasmin, D.; Kamal, A.-H. M.; Islam, M. T.; Islam, S. S.; Islam, A.; Islam, M. S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research Bangladesh
after.abstract: Introduction Mobile poultry vending and slaughtering practices in Bangladesh pose potential public health risks due to poor hygiene, unsafe waste disposal, and close human-animal interactions. Limited data exist on these practices and feasible interventions to improve biosecurity among mobile poultry vendors. Methods This mixed-method study was conducted in three phases across four sub-districts in three districts. Phase 1 involved 416 hours of structured observation, 40 in-depth vendor interviews, and 40 informal customer interviews. Phase 2 involved the development and pilot testing of an intervention package, including poultry killing cones, hand sanitizers, disinfectants, and a hygiene pamphlet, with 10 vendors. Phase 3 implemented the intervention among 20 vendors for one month, followed by 94 hours of observation and 17 customer interviews. Result Phase 1 found 1,959 slaughtering events with no use of personal protective equipment; slaughtering occurred in plastic jars (58%), directly on roads (21%), and roadside drains (11%). Seventy percent of vendors reported discarding slaughtering waste directly into the environment, while 78% reported not knowing how poultry diseases could spread to other animals or humans. During Phase 2, 9/10 vendors considered the killing cone useful, although bicycle users reported challenges related to weight and balance; the cone was subsequently modified. During Phase 3, 294 poultry were observed being slaughtered, with 79% using killing cones. Waste was stored in cone-attached boxes in 97% of cone uses, and vendors used hand sanitizer before eating in 75% of observed instances. Among 17 interviewed customers, 88% recognized the cones role in safer waste disposal and 53% considered it useful overall. Conclusion This study highlights major hygiene and biosecurity gaps and demonstrates that low-cost, targeted interventions may improve biosecurity practices among mobile poultry vendors and reduce opportunities for environmental contamination in informal slaughter settings.

Methods: We performed untargeted urinary metabolomics in 314 infants (<29 weeks gestational age) at two time points between postnatal days 5-15 and 23-32, with detailed time-series for 28 infants. We compared metabolite levels between infants with and without BPD at 36 weeks postmenstrual age using logistic regression and pathway enrichment analysis. A stratified analysis by nutrition type was performed at 23-32 days. Results: Among the 913 analyzed urinary metabolites, 23 and 68 were nominally associated with BPD between postnatal days 5-15 and 23-32, respectively (p<0.05). We found enrichment in the lactoyl amino acid sub-pathway (5-15 days; p=0.005, q=0.4) and xanthine metabolism and fatty acid metabolism (23-32 days; p[≤]0.002, q<0.1). Most BPD-differential metabolites were lower in infants with BPD at days 23-32 (OR=7.1, p=2x10-6), with similar patterns among infants receiving parenteral (OR=9.2, p=7x10-7) and full enteral nutrition (OR=6.1, p=0.003). Twenty-four metabolites, including vitamins C, B1, and B6, were lower in infants on parenteral nutrition with BPD at postnatal days 23-32. Discussion: BPD in extremely premature infants was associated with lower levels of vitamin-related metabolites and dysregulation of lactoyl amino acids, xanthine, and fatty acid metabolism. BPD-differential metabolites were lower in infants with BPD during the fourth week of life, potentially related to higher energy demand, metabolic dysregulation, insufficient nutrient availability, and/or impaired intestinal absorption.

after.authors: Poffley, R. C.; Soper, R.; de Lorenzo, D.; Nyamapfeni, P.; Madziva, K.; Masvikeni, C.; Meck, K.; Chimhuya, S.; Gannon, H.; Heys, M.; Fitzgerald, F.; Mangiza, M.

after.abstract: Reducing neonatal mortality remains a global priority, yet progress has stalled in many low-resource settings. Low-cost interventions such as delayed cord clamping (DCC) and early skin to skin care (ESSC) are known to reduce neonatal morbidity and mortality but implementation remains inconsistent. Prior to project initiation, Sally Mugabe Central Hospital, Zimbabwe's busiest tertiary maternity unit had no documented DCC or ESSC conducted with practice limited by staffing pressures and infrastructural challenges. We aimed to implement a context-specific Golden Hour care bundle to improve newborn care during the first hour after birth. Using quality improvement (QI) methodology we designed interventions alongside maternity staff, including multidisciplinary training, embedded clinical support, regular feedback, leadership engagement and equipment provision. Real-time progress was tracked using the Neotree digital data tool over 12 months (November 2024-October 2025). The primary outcome was documented DCC and ESSC in eligible infants. An analysis of neonatal mortality among a subset of admitted inborn infants was also carried out. A total of 207 healthcare workers and 87 student midwives received formal training. Over 12 months, 15,292 eligible infants (81.1%) received DCC and 14,351 (76.1%) received ESSC with sustained implementation between 82-91% (DCC) and 72-85% (ESSC) for the final seven months of the project. Targeted PDSA cycles increased uptake in low birthweight infants and babies born by caesarean section. Logistic regression analysis of infants admitted to the neonatal unit demonstrated a trend to reduction in crude mortality for eligible infants receiving both interventions but this did not reach statistical significance. A multifaceted, context-specific QI programme successfully embedded evidence-based Golden Hour practices in a high-volume, resource-constrained maternity unit. Combining education, equipment, clinical support and continuous data feedback achieved sustained change in practice and a trend towards improved survival.

after.title: Preprint: Pre- and postnatal environmental lithium exposure and adolescent neurodevelopment: a tooth-biomarker study
after.authors: König, M.; Marshall, A. T.; Adise, S.; Kan, E.; McConnell, R.; Martinez, M.; Midya, V.; Arora, M.; Sowell, E. R.
after.abstract: Lithium is a naturally occurring element found in drinking water, and its environmental presence is rising with demand for batteries. Yet evidence on lithium comes almost entirely from adults, ecological studies, or medical treatment, leaving the effects of prenatal and early postnatal environmental exposure unknown. We laser-mapped lithium in shed baby teeth, which preserve a record of exposure around birth (-12 to +13 weeks), from 448 U.S. youth in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study and tested associations with brain structure, cognition, and behavior at ages 9-10. Higher lithium was found in children of less-educated caregivers and from more deprived neighborhoods. Higher lithium was also linked to thicker cortices, varying surface area, mostly smaller subcortical volumes, poorer reading and language ability, and more externalizing problems, with associations varying by caregiver education. Early-life environmental lithium exposure may therefore be socioeconomically patterned and contribute to disparities in neurodevelopment, warranting environmental health surveillance.
